title: Energy giant’s security warning after data hack
full_text:
Australia’s largest energy company has given a warning about the country’s cyber security just months after the data of 900,000 customers was stolen.
In his address to shareholders at the Origin Energy annual general meeting, chairman Scott Perkins said cyber attacks remained a real threat.
“Unfortunately, individuals and businesses, no matter where they are around the world, face a growing threat from this sort of criminally motivated cyber activity,” he said “The threat environment is constantly evolving, and we will have to work hard to continue to protect the security of our systems and our customers’ information.” Mr Perkins’ comments follow a cyber attack in July when the data of up to 900,000 of Origin’s more than four million customers was stolen.
Bank details, ID documents, and government concession numbers are among the highly sensitive information exposed.
Up to 15,000 people had numbers associated with government concessions or schemes taken in the July 2 data breach. Sixty had their full bank account numbers stolen and another 100 had information from identifying documents taken.
Mr Perkins said Origin would continue to support affected customers. “Customers place enormous trust in Origin to protect their information, and we do not take that for granted,” Mr Perkins said. “We have apologised to customers who were affected while providing support, and have taken a number of steps to enhance the security of our systems to prevent future incidents of this kind.” He said there was no evidence that any data was published on the dark web but urged customers to remain vigilant to scams.
Origin previously said it was working with the Australian Cyber Security Centre, the National Office of Cyber Security and the Australian Federal Police after tracing the cyber hack to the Philippines.
The company’s chief executive Frank Calabria spoke before the annual general meeting about the importance of cheap power for households and the energy transition.
“Energy underpins everything in our economy – the cost of living for every household, the competitiveness of every business and Australia’s productivity,” he said. He said the next phase of the transition depended on large-scale infrastructure, the build out of transmission lines, renewable projects, firming capacity and energy storage.
